editorNote: The week belongs to IBM PC software: Lotus 1-2-3 reaches buyers while home-computer shelves keep mixing adventures, arcade conversions, and practical utilities.
morningLine: Software counters are talking spreadsheets, game shelves are still bright with Atari and Commodore boxes, and Tootsie keeps packing theaters.

lead.headline: Lotus 1-2-3 reaches IBM PC desks
lead.summary: Lotus Development released Lotus 1-2-3 on January 26, 1983, tying spreadsheet, charting, and database features into one IBM PC package that quickly became a defining business reason to buy a PC-compatible machine.

computerItems.title: IBM PC software gets its showcase app
computerItems.summary: Lotus 1-2-3 arrived as an integrated spreadsheet package for the IBM PC, a sharper pitch than single-purpose office programs and a sign that PC business software was becoming the hardware story.

computerItems.title: Commodore 64 game catalogs widen
computerItems.summary: 1983 releases for the Commodore 64 and Atari 8-bit lines include shooters, adventures, and strategy titles such as Attack of the Mutant Camels, Dragonriders of Pern, and Gateway to Apshai.

computerItems.title: Arcade-to-home demand stays visible
computerItems.summary: Retail shelves and magazine ads continue to lean on recognizable arcade action while publishers court home-computer buyers with disk and cartridge editions.

computerItems.title: The spreadsheet fight moves beyond VisiCalc
computerItems.summary: Lotus 1-2-3 enters a market VisiCalc made famous, but with IBM PC focus and integrated graphics/database features that changed buyer expectations.
